about: Structural Mechanics 1 (CIVE40006) is a 5-ECTS core module running through the Autumn and Spring terms of Year 1 of Imperial's MEng Civil Engineering, and the first of the structural mechanics modules that continue into later years. We could not find a published syllabus or topic list for it, so the topics here are a standard first-year course on statically determinate structures (equilibrium, trusses, axial members, beams, bending, deflection and buckling), built from the module's title and the department's description, not from an official topic list. The programme specification gives a 32% coursework and 68% examination split for Year 1 as a whole; the module's own assessment could not be confirmed.
topics: Shear force and bending moment diagrams

notes.body:
Structural mechanics starts with equilibrium. A structure, and every part cut from it, must be in equilibrium under the loads and the support reactions.

Equations of equilibrium (plane structures)
- ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 about any point.
These give three independent equations for each rigid body. Moments can be taken about any point; choosing a point through which several unknowns pass removes them from the equation.

Free body diagrams
Draw the structure (or a part of it) isolated from its surroundings, with every external load and every reaction or internal force shown, including assumed directions. A free body diagram is the most important step in any statics problem; most errors come from a missing force.

Supports and the reactions they provide
- Roller (or sliding bearing): one force, perpendicular to the surface.
- Pin (hinge): two force components; no moment.
- Fixed (built-in, encastré): two forces and a moment.
- An internal hinge in a beam or frame carries force but no moment, adding one extra condition (M = 0 at the hinge).

Loads
- Point loads (kN), uniformly distributed loads w (kN/m), varying loads, and applied moments (kN m).
- For reactions, a UDL can be replaced by its resultant wL acting at the centre of the loaded length (but not when finding internal moments within the loaded length).

Worked example: beam with an overhang
A beam is pinned at A, on a roller at B 6 m from A, and overhangs 2 m to a free end C. It carries 10 kN/m from A to B and a 20 kN point load at C.
- Moments about A: R_B × 6 = (10 × 6) × 3 + 20 × 8 = 340, so R_B = 56.67 kN.
- Vertical equilibrium: R_A = 60 + 20 − 56.67 = 23.33 kN.
- Check with moments about B: R_A × 6 = 60 × 3 − 20 × 2 = 140, giving 23.33 kN.

Static determinacy
A structure is statically determinate if all reactions and internal forces can be found from equilibrium alone.
- A single plane beam or rigid body: determinate if it has exactly 3 independent reaction components (properly arranged). Each extra reaction adds one degree of indeterminacy: a propped cantilever (fixed + roller, 4 components) is indeterminate to degree 1; a beam fixed at both ends (6 components) to degree 3 (often 2 if axial forces are ignored).
- Plane pin-jointed truss: degree of indeterminacy = m + r − 2j.
- Plane rigid-jointed frame: degree = 3m + r − 3j (minus one for each internal hinge release).
Fewer unknowns than equations means a mechanism; the count is also not enough on its own, since a badly arranged support (for example three parallel rollers) can still allow movement (geometric instability).

Why it matters
Determinate structures can be analysed by statics alone and are not stressed by settlement or temperature change; indeterminate ones need compatibility and stiffness, but offer redundancy and usually smaller moments.

Exam tips: always check reactions with an equation you did not use to find them, and state the degree of indeterminacy with the counting formula you used.

Trusses (roof trusses, bridge girders, transmission towers, cranes) carry load efficiently because their members work mainly in direct tension or compression.

Modelling assumptions
- Members are straight and joined by frictionless pins.
- Loads act only at the joints.
- Each member is therefore a two-force member with an axial force only.
Real trusses usually have bolted or welded joints, so small secondary bending moments exist, but the pin-jointed model gives the primary forces well.

Determinacy
For a plane truss with m members, j joints and r reactions: m + r = 2j for a determinate truss (if the arrangement is stable). Triangulation is the key: a truss built up by adding two members and one joint at a time to a triangle is stable and determinate.

Method of joints
Isolate a joint, show all bar forces as tensions (pulling away from the joint), and apply ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0. Start at a joint with at most two unknowns, usually a support once the reactions are known.

Method of sections
Cut through at most three members (not all meeting at one point), and apply the three equilibrium equations to one side. Take moments about the intersection of two cut members to find the third directly. This is the fastest way to find a single member force in the middle of a truss.

Worked example: Pratt truss
Span 8 m, four panels of 2 m, height 2 m. Bottom joints A, B, C, D, E at x = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 m; top joints F, G, H above B, C, D. Diagonals run from A up to F, F down to C, C up to H and H down to E. Loads of 10 kN act at B, C and D. By symmetry R_A = R_E = 15 kN. Check the count: m = 13, j = 8, r = 3, so m + r = 16 = 2j.
- Section through FG, FC and BC, left part:
  - moments about F: F_BC × 2 = 15 × 2, so F_BC = 15 kN (tension);
  - moments about C: F_FG × 2 = −(15 × 4 − 10 × 2), so F_FG = −20 kN (compression);
  - vertical forces: 15 − 10 − F_FC sin 45° = 0, so F_FC = 7.07 kN (tension).
- Joint A: vertical equilibrium gives F_AF sin 45° = −15, so F_AF = −21.2 kN (compression); horizontal gives F_AB = 15 kN (tension).
- Joint B: vertical equilibrium gives F_BF = 10 kN (tension), carrying the joint load up.
- Joint G (unloaded, with FG and GH collinear): the vertical CG is a zero-force member.

Patterns worth remembering
- Under gravity loads on a simply supported truss, the top chord is in compression and the bottom chord in tension.
- In a Pratt truss the interior diagonals are in tension (in the example above the inclined end members AF and HE act as end posts and are in compression) and the verticals in compression or tension depending on the load positions; in a Howe truss (diagonals sloping the other way) the diagonals are in compression.
- Compression members must be checked for buckling as well as stress, which is why long diagonals are best arranged to be in tension.
- Zero-force members still matter: they brace compression members and carry loads in other load cases.

Member stress and extension
Once the force F in a member is known, its stress is F/A and its extension FL/(AE).

Exam tips: draw the section clearly, label assumed tensions, and use the sign of the answer; check one joint you did not use as a final test.

notes.h: Axially loaded members: stress, strain and Hooke's law
notes.body:
Columns, ties, cables, hangers and truss members carry mainly axial load. Their analysis introduces stress, strain and material stiffness.

Definitions
- Direct stress σ = N/A (N/mm² = MPa). Tension positive.
- Direct strain ε = δ/L.
- Hooke's law: σ = Eε within the elastic range, so δ = NL/(EA). EA is the axial rigidity and EA/L the axial stiffness.
- Poisson's ratio ν = −lateral strain/axial strain (about 0.3 for steel and 0.1–0.2 for concrete, approximate).
- Typical E values (approximate): structural steel 200–210 GPa; concrete 25–40 GPa depending on strength and age; timber along the grain 7–15 GPa.

Stress–strain behaviour of structural materials
- Mild steel: linear up to a clear yield point (e.g. 275 or 355 MPa for common structural grades, named S275 and S355), then a yield plateau and strain hardening. Ductile.
- Concrete: strong in compression, weak in tension (tensile strength roughly a tenth of compressive, approximate), so it is reinforced with steel where tension occurs.
- Timber: anisotropic; much stiffer and stronger along the grain.

Members of more than one material
When two materials are bonded together and strain equally (reinforced concrete, composite sections), use:
- compatibility: ε_steel = ε_concrete;
- equilibrium: σ_s A_s + σ_c A_c = N;
- so ε = N/(E_s A_s + E_c A_c).
The modular ratio n = E_s/E_c lets you convert to an equivalent area of one material: A_equivalent = A_c + nA_s.
Example: a 300 × 300 mm column with four 25 mm steel bars (A_s = 1963 mm²; A_c = 88 040 mm²) carries 1500 kN, with E_s = 200 GPa and E_c = 30 GPa. ε = 1.5 × 10⁶/(200 000 × 1963 + 30 000 × 88 040) = 4.94 × 10⁻⁴, so σ_s = 98.9 MPa and σ_c = 14.8 MPa. The steel, only about 2% of the area, carries about 194 kN (13% of the load).

Statically indeterminate axial problems
A bar fixed at both ends and loaded part-way along, or a load shared by several cables of different stiffness, needs equilibrium plus a compatibility condition (e.g. the total length change is zero).

Thermal effects
A free member changes length by αLΔT (α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K for steel and roughly 10 × 10⁻⁶ /K for concrete, approximate, which is why they work well together). If restrained, a stress EαΔT develops. A continuous welded rail (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K) heated 30 K above its stress-free temperature develops about 72 MPa compression.

Self-weight of a hanging member
A cable or bar of density ρ and length L hanging under its own weight has maximum stress ρgL at the top and extension ρgL²/(2E), half of what the same total weight would cause if applied at the bottom. For a 100 m steel cable (ρ = 7850 kg/m³): σ_max = 7.7 MPa and δ = 1.9 mm.

Exam tips: for indeterminate and composite members, write equilibrium, compatibility and the material law as three separate labelled lines; and keep units consistent (N, mm, MPa).

notes.h: Shear force and bending moment diagrams
notes.body:
Beams are the most common structural members. The shear force V and bending moment M at each section determine the stresses, so drawing their diagrams is a core skill.

Definitions
- Shear force at a section: the algebraic sum of transverse forces on one side of the section.
- Bending moment at a section: the algebraic sum of moments of the forces on one side about the section.
- Convention used here: sagging moment (tension at the bottom) is positive; shear is positive when the left-hand part tends to move up relative to the right. Different textbooks differ, so state yours.

Relationships between load, shear and moment (w downward positive)
- dV/dx = −w and dM/dx = V.
- So the change in M between two sections equals the area under the SFD between them.
- M is a local maximum or minimum where V = 0 (or where V changes sign at a point load).
- Point load: step in V, kink in M. Applied couple: step in M.
- No load: V constant, M linear. UDL: V linear, M parabolic.

Procedure
1. Find the reactions (and check them).
2. Work along the beam from one end, plotting V just left and right of each point load and support.
3. Find M at supports, point loads, and where V = 0.
4. Join the points with straight lines or parabolas as the loading requires.

Worked example: beam with an overhang
Pin at A (x = 0), roller at B (x = 6 m), overhang to C (x = 8 m). UDL 10 kN/m on AB; 20 kN at C. Reactions R_A = 23.33 kN, R_B = 56.67 kN.
Shear force:
- V = 23.33 − 10x on AB: 23.33 kN at A, zero at x = 2.33 m, −36.67 kN just left of B.
- At B it jumps up by 56.67 to +20 kN, constant to C, then drops to zero at the free end.
Bending moment:
- M = 23.33x − 5x² on AB.
- Maximum sagging moment where V = 0: M = 23.33 × 2.333 − 5 × 2.333² = 27.2 kN m.
- At B: M = −20 × 2 = −40 kN m (hogging), from the overhang load.
- M = 0 again at x = 4.67 m: this is a point of contraflexure, where the moment changes sign and the beam's curvature reverses.
The largest moment in magnitude is the 40 kN m hogging moment over the support, so the top of the beam is most highly stressed in tension there; this matters for materials such as reinforced concrete, where steel must be placed on the tension face.

Cantilevers and standard cases
- Cantilever with end load P: M = −PL at the support (hogging).
- Cantilever with UDL: M = −wL²/2 at the support.
- Simply supported with UDL: M_max = wL²/8; with a central point load: PL/4.

Exam tips: always mark numerical values at key points, label sagging/hogging, and use the area-under-SFD check: here the area from A to the zero-shear point is ½ × 23.33 × 2.333 = 27.2 kN m, matching M_max.

Elastic bending theory
For an initially straight, prismatic, linear-elastic beam in which plane sections remain plane:
M/I = σ/y = E/R
- y is measured from the neutral axis, which passes through the centroid of the cross-section.
- Stress varies linearly from zero at the neutral axis to maxima at the extreme fibres.
- Sagging: compression on top, tension at the bottom; hogging: the reverse.

Section properties
- Centroid: ȳ = ΣAᵢyᵢ/ΣAᵢ for a section made of simple shapes.
- Second moment of area: rectangle bd³/12 about its centroid; circle πd⁴/64.
- Parallel axis theorem: I = ΣIᵢ + ΣAᵢhᵢ², where hᵢ is the distance from each part's centroid to the neutral axis.
- Hollow and I-sections: subtract the missing parts, e.g. a rectangular hollow section of outer size B × D and inner b × d has I = (BD³ − bd³)/12.
- Elastic section modulus Z = I/y_max, so σ_max = M/Z. For a rectangle, Z = bd²/6.
- Radius of gyration r = √(I/A) (used in buckling).

Why shape matters
Bending stress is largest far from the neutral axis, so material placed there works hardest. I-beams and box sections put most of their area in the flanges, giving a large I for little weight. Increasing depth is very effective: Z ∝ d² and I ∝ d³ for a rectangle.

Worked example 1: sizing a timber joist
A floor joist spans 4 m, simply supported, with a UDL of 2 kN/m. M_max = wL²/8 = 4 kN m. With an allowable bending stress of 10 MPa (illustrative), the required Z = 4 × 10⁶/10 = 4 × 10⁵ mm³. For a 75 mm wide joist, bd²/6 ≥ 4 × 10⁵ gives d ≥ 179 mm, so a 75 × 200 mm joist would be chosen (Z = 5 × 10⁵ mm³, σ = 8 MPa).

Worked example 2: rectangular hollow section
Outer 100 mm wide × 200 mm deep, wall 10 mm (inner 80 × 180 mm).
- I = (100 × 200³ − 80 × 180³)/12 = 2.78 × 10⁷ mm⁴.
- Z = I/100 = 2.78 × 10⁵ mm³.
- For a steel with design stress 165 MPa (illustrative), the moment capacity in elastic bending is 165 × 2.78 × 10⁵ = 45.8 kN m.

Unsymmetrical sections
For a T-section or a channel bent about its axis of symmetry, the neutral axis is not at mid-depth: find ȳ first, then I using the parallel axis theorem, then check both extreme fibres. This is important for materials weaker in tension than compression.

Beyond elastic bending (background)
Steel beams can carry more than the first-yield moment: as yielding spreads through the section the moment rises towards the plastic moment M_p = σ_y Z_p, where Z_p is the plastic section modulus (1.5 times Z for a rectangle). Design codes such as Eurocode 3 use this reserve. Shear stresses in beams are found from τ = VAȳ/(Ib), and are usually largest at the neutral axis.

Exam tips: state the neutral axis position and I clearly with units (mm⁴), use y from the neutral axis (not from the base) in σ = My/I, and say which face is in tension.

Serviceability, meaning that a structure does not sag, vibrate or crack its finishes unacceptably, often governs design as much as strength. Deflections come from the curvature produced by bending.

Moment–curvature relationship
From M/I = E/R and, for small slopes, 1/R ≈ d²v/dx²:
EI d²v/dx² = M(x)
with v upward and sagging M positive. EI is the flexural rigidity.

Double integration
1. Write M(x).
2. Integrate once for the slope EI dv/dx, and again for the deflection EI v, adding constants C₁ and C₂.
3. Use boundary conditions: v = 0 at pins and rollers; v = 0 and dv/dx = 0 at a fixed end; dv/dx = 0 at a line of symmetry.

Macaulay's method
For beams with several point loads, write a single expression for M using Macaulay brackets ⟨x − a⟩ (zero when x < a). Integrate brackets as units, ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ → ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1), so only two constants are needed for the whole beam.

Worked example: four-point loading
A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries 10 kN at each third point (x = 2 m and 4 m); EI = 20 000 kN m². R_A = R_B = 10 kN.
- EI v″ = 10x − 10⟨x − 2⟩ − 10⟨x − 4⟩.
- EI v = (10/6)x³ − (10/6)⟨x − 2⟩³ − (10/6)⟨x − 4⟩³ + C₁x + C₂.
- v(0) = 0 gives C₂ = 0. v(6) = 0: (10/6)(216 − 64 − 8) + 6C₁ = 0, so 240 + 6C₁ = 0 and C₁ = −40 kN m².
- At mid-span (x = 3): EI v = 45 − 1.67 + 0 − 120 = −76.7 kN m³, so v = −76.7/20 000 = −3.83 mm.
- Check: the standard result 23PL³/(648EI) = 23 × 10 × 216/(648 × 20 000) = 3.83 mm.

Standard results (magnitudes)
- Cantilever, end load: PL³/(3EI). Cantilever, UDL: wL⁴/(8EI).
- Simply supported, central load: PL³/(48EI). Simply supported, UDL: 5wL⁴/(384EI).
Example: a 2 m cantilever with 5 kN/m and EI = 5000 kN m² deflects 5 × 2⁴/(8 × 5000) = 0.002 m = 2 mm at the tip.

Superposition
For linear-elastic, small-deflection behaviour, deflections from separate loads add. Complex loadings can often be built from the standard cases.

Deflection limits (background)
Design codes and guidance set limits such as span/250 to span/360 for floor beams under various loads, depending on the finishes and the code; these are serviceability checks, not strength checks.

Indeterminate beams (link to later modules)
Deflection equations also give the extra equation needed for indeterminate beams. For a propped cantilever with a UDL, requiring the deflection at the prop to be zero gives a prop reaction of 3wL/8.

Exam tips: state your sign convention and boundary conditions explicitly, keep Macaulay brackets intact while integrating, and work in consistent units (kN and m with EI in kN m² is often easiest).

A slender member in compression can fail by buckling sideways at a load far below that needed to crush the material. Buckling is a stability failure, governed by stiffness (E and I) and length rather than strength.

Euler buckling load
For an ideal, initially straight, pin-ended, linear-elastic strut of length L:
P_cr = π²EI/L²
- I is the smallest second moment of area of the section, because the strut buckles about its weakest axis.
- At P_cr the straight form becomes unstable and the strut deflects into a half sine wave.

Effective length
Other end conditions are handled with an effective length L_e = kL (theoretical values):
- Pinned–pinned: L_e = L.
- Fixed–free (flagpole or cantilever column): L_e = 2L, so P_cr is a quarter of the pinned value.
- Fixed–pinned: L_e ≈ 0.7L, roughly doubling P_cr.
- Fixed–fixed: L_e = 0.5L, four times the pinned value.
Design codes use somewhat larger factors for "fixed" ends because real connections are never perfectly rigid (background).

Slenderness ratio and Euler stress
- Radius of gyration r = √(I/A).
- Slenderness ratio λ = L_e/r.
- Euler critical stress σ_cr = P_cr/A = π²E/λ².
A strut fails by buckling if σ_cr is below the yield (squash) stress, i.e. if λ is greater than about π√(E/σ_y). For steel with E = 200 GPa and σ_y = 275 MPa this limiting slenderness is about 85. Stocky columns (low λ) fail by yielding or crushing; slender ones by elastic buckling.

Worked example
A pin-ended steel tube, outside diameter 60 mm, inside 50 mm, length 3 m; E = 200 GPa, σ_y = 275 MPa.
- A = π(60² − 50²)/4 = 864 mm²; I = π(60⁴ − 50⁴)/64 = 3.29 × 10⁵ mm⁴; r = √(I/A) = 19.5 mm.
- λ = 3000/19.5 = 154, well above 85, so elastic buckling governs.
- P_cr = π² × 200 000 × 3.29 × 10⁵/3000² = 72.2 kN (σ_cr = 83.6 MPa).
- The squash load σ_y A = 238 kN is more than three times larger, so treating the tube as limited by yield would be dangerously unsafe.
- If the same tube were fixed at the base and free at the top, P_cr would be 72.2/4 = 18.1 kN.

Real columns
Real struts have initial crookedness, eccentric loading and residual stresses, so they fail below both the Euler load and the squash load, with the greatest reduction near the transition slenderness. Design methods (for example the Perry–Robertson approach underlying steel column curves in codes) account for these imperfections (background).

Improving buckling resistance
- Shorten the effective length with bracing or stiffer end connections.
- Increase I without adding much area: tubes and hollow sections are efficient because their material is far from the centroid in every direction.
- E matters, not strength: high-strength steel gives no benefit to a very slender strut.

Exam tips: always use the minimum I, identify the end conditions before choosing L_e, and compare the Euler load with the squash load to decide which mode governs.

cards.b: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 about any point: three independent equations per rigid body.

cards.f: Reactions at a pin, roller and fixed support
cards.b: Roller: 1 force. Pin: 2 forces. Fixed: 2 forces and a moment.
Transmits force but not moment; adds one equation (M = 0 at the hinge), reducing the degree of indeterminacy by one.

cards.f: Degree of indeterminacy: rigid-jointed plane frame
cards.b: 3m + r − 3j (minus releases such as internal hinges).
One: 4 reaction components (fixed end 3, roller 1) against 3 equations.
A structure that satisfies the counting rule but can still move, e.g. all reactions parallel or concurrent.
wL acting at the centroid (mid-point) of the loaded length.
Members carry mainly axial force, so the whole cross-section is used at a uniform stress, unlike bending where only the outer fibres are highly stressed.
m + r = 2j for a statically determinate plane truss (if stable).

cards.f: Method of sections: which moment centre?
cards.b: The intersection point of two of the cut members, so the third member's force is found from one equation.
Simply supported truss: top chord compression, bottom chord tension.
Pratt: interior diagonals slope down towards mid-span and are in tension under gravity load. Howe: diagonals slope the other way and are in compression.

cards.f: Zero-force member at an unloaded joint
cards.b: If two members are collinear and a third is not, the third carries zero force; if only two non-collinear members meet, both are zero.
δ = FL/(AE), with F the axial force from the truss analysis.
δ = NL/(EA); EA is the axial rigidity and EA/L the stiffness.
n = E_s/E_c; steel area is multiplied by n to give an equivalent concrete area (transformed section).
Equal strain in both materials: ε = N/(E₁A₁ + E₂A₂), then σᵢ = Eᵢε.

cards.f: Thermal stress in a restrained member
cards.b: σ = EαΔT (compression on heating, tension on cooling) when the free expansion αLΔT is prevented.
Maximum stress ρgL at the top; extension ρgL²/(2E).

cards.f: Typical E for steel and concrete (approximate)
cards.b: Steel 200–210 GPa; concrete about 25–40 GPa.
Its tensile strength is only roughly a tenth of its compressive strength (approximate), so steel bars carry the tension.
A point where the bending moment changes sign (passes through zero), so the beam's curvature reverses.
The change in bending moment between two sections equals the area under the shear force diagram between them.

cards.f: Where is the maximum bending moment?
cards.b: Where the shear force is zero or changes sign (also check supports and free ends of overhangs).
Bending that makes the beam concave downwards, with tension on top; typical over supports of continuous or overhanging beams.

cards.f: Effect of an applied couple on the BMD
cards.b: A step change in bending moment equal to the couple; no change in shear force.
−wL²/2 (hogging), with support shear wL.

cards.f: Shape of the BMD under a UDL
cards.b: Parabolic (second order), because V varies linearly.
M/I = σ/y = E/R, with y measured from the neutral axis.
Z = bd²/6, so σ_max = 6M/(bd²).

cards.f: I of a rectangular hollow section
cards.b: I = (BD³ − bd³)/12 using outer (B × D) and inner (b × d) dimensions, both symmetric about the same axis.
ȳ = ΣAᵢyᵢ/ΣAᵢ, measured from a chosen datum.
I = I_c + Ah² for each part; sum over all parts about the neutral axis.
M_p = σ_y Z_p; for a rectangle Z_p = bd²/4 = 1.5Z.
τ = VAȳ/(Ib), where Aȳ is the first moment of the area beyond the level considered; usually maximum at the neutral axis.
EI d²v/dx² = M(x) (small slopes); EI is the flexural rigidity.
Pin/roller: v = 0. Fixed end: v = 0 and dv/dx = 0. Line of symmetry: dv/dx = 0.

cards.f: Simply supported beam, UDL: mid-span deflection

cards.b: wL⁴/(8EI).

cards.f: Simply supported, equal loads at third points: mid-span deflection
cards.b: 23PL³/(648EI) for loads P at L/3 and 2L/3.
⟨x − a⟩ = 0 for x < a; integrate as a unit, ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ → ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1).

cards.f: Prop reaction of a propped cantilever with UDL
cards.b: 3wL/8, found from the compatibility condition of zero deflection at the prop.
P_cr = π²EI/L², using the minimum second moment of area.
Pinned–pinned 1.0L; fixed–free 2.0L; fixed–pinned ≈ 0.7L; fixed–fixed 0.5L.
λ = L_e/r, with radius of gyration r = √(I/A).
σ_cr = π²E/λ².

cards.f: Limiting slenderness between yielding and buckling
cards.b: λ ≈ π√(E/σ_y); about 85 for E = 200 GPa and σ_y = 275 MPa.
Material far from the centroid in all directions gives a high I (and r) for the area, with no weak axis.

cards.f: Why real columns fail below the Euler load
cards.b: Initial crookedness, load eccentricity and residual stresses cause bending and early yielding.

questions.q: A beam is pinned at A and supported on a roller at B, 6 m from A, and overhangs 2 m beyond B to C. It carries 10 kN/m over AB and 20 kN at C. What is the reaction at B?
questions.why: Moments about A: 6R_B = 60 × 3 + 20 × 8 = 340, so R_B = 56.7 kN. 23.3 kN is R_A, the other reaction. 40.0 kN is half the total load, which would only be right for a symmetric case. 36.7 kN comes from using the 2 m overhang as the lever arm of the 20 kN load ((180 + 20 × 2)/6), measuring it from B instead of from A, which is 8 m away.

questions.q: A plane beam is built in at one end and rests on rollers at two further points along its length. What is its degree of static indeterminacy (counting axial reactions)?
questions.why: The fixed end gives 3 reactions and each roller 1, so r = 5; with 3 equilibrium equations the degree is 5 − 3 = 2. 1 is the result for a propped cantilever with only one roller. 3 comes from counting one of the rollers as a pin (r = 6). 0 would mean the beam could be solved by statics alone, which needs exactly 3 reaction components.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a statically determinate and a statically indeterminate structure, and give one practical advantage of each.
markScheme: Determinate: reactions and internal forces found from equilibrium alone (unknowns = equations)
Indeterminate: more unknowns than equations; needs compatibility and member stiffness
Advantage of determinate: unaffected by settlement, temperature or lack of fit; simple analysis
Advantage of indeterminate: redundancy (alternative load paths) and generally smaller moments/deflections
questions.modelAnswer: In a statically determinate structure the number of unknown reactions and internal forces equals the number of independent equilibrium equations, so everything can be found from statics alone. In an indeterminate structure there are more unknowns than equations, so compatibility of deformations and the stiffness of the members must also be used. Determinate structures are simpler to analyse and are not stressed by support settlement, temperature change or small fabrication errors, because they can adjust freely. Indeterminate structures have redundancy: if one member or support is damaged, loads can find another path, and continuity usually reduces the peak bending moments and deflections, allowing lighter members.

questions.q: In the Pratt truss of span 8 m (four 2 m panels, height 2 m, 10 kN at each of the three interior bottom joints), what is the force in the top chord member FG over the second panel?
questions.why: Cut through FG, FC and BC and take moments about C: 15 × 4 − 10 × 2 = 40 kN m, divided by the 2 m height gives 20 kN; the top chord is in compression. Tension has the wrong sense for a top chord under gravity load. 15 kN is the bottom chord force in the same panel (moments about F). 30 kN ignores the 10 kN load at B in the moment about C (15 × 4/2).

questions.q: A plane truss has 11 members and 7 joints and is supported by two pins. How is it classified?
options: Statically indeterminate to the first degree
questions.why: Two pins give r = 4, so m + r = 15 against 2j = 14: one more unknown than equations, indeterminate to degree 1. 'Determinate' results from treating one support as a roller (r = 3). 'A mechanism' would need m + r < 2j, e.g. by forgetting the reactions. 'Third degree' comes from counting each pin as giving three reactions (r = 6, so m + r = 17).

questions.q: For the same Pratt truss (span 8 m, panels 2 m, height 2 m, 10 kN at B, C and D), use the method of joints at A and B to find the forces in AF, AB and BF, and explain why member CG carries no force.
markScheme: Reactions R_A = R_E = 15 kN
Joint A vertical: F_AF sin 45° + 15 = 0, F_AF = −21.2 kN (compression)
Joint A horizontal: F_AB + F_AF cos 45° = 0, F_AB = 15 kN (tension)
Joint B vertical: F_BF − 10 = 0, F_BF = 10 kN (tension)
Joint G: FG and GH collinear and no external load, so CG = 0
questions.modelAnswer: By symmetry R_A = R_E = (3 × 10)/2 = 15 kN. Joint A has the reaction, AB (horizontal) and AF (at 45°). Vertically: F_AF sin 45° + 15 = 0, so F_AF = −21.2 kN, i.e. 21.2 kN compression. Horizontally: F_AB + F_AF cos 45° = 0, so F_AB = 15 kN tension. Joint B has AB and BC (collinear, horizontal), BF (vertical) and the 10 kN load. Vertically: F_BF − 10 = 0, so F_BF = 10 kN tension: the vertical hangs the load from the top joint. At joint G, members FG and GH are collinear and horizontal, there is no external load, and CG is the only member with a vertical component, so vertical equilibrium forces F_CG = 0.

questions.q: A continuous welded steel rail (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K) is fully restrained and heated 30 K above its stress-free temperature. What stress develops?
questions.why: σ = EαΔT = 200 000 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 30 = 72 MPa, compressive because the rail wants to expand but cannot. Tension would occur on cooling below the stress-free temperature. 7.2 MPa is a factor-of-ten slip, taking α as 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ /K. 2.4 MPa is Eα alone, forgetting to multiply by the 30 K temperature change.

questions.q: A 300 × 300 mm reinforced concrete column has 1963 mm² of steel (E_s = 200 GPa) and E_c = 30 GPa. It carries 1500 kN. What is the stress in the concrete?
questions.why: Equal strain: ε = 1.5 × 10⁶/(200 000 × 1963 + 30 000 × 88 037) = 4.94 × 10⁻⁴, so σ_c = 30 000 × 4.94 × 10⁻⁴ = 14.8 MPa. 16.7 MPa divides the load by the gross area 90 000 mm², ignoring the stiffer steel. 98.9 MPa is the stress in the steel. 17.0 MPa divides the load by the net concrete area alone, assuming the steel carries nothing.

questions.q: A 100 m long steel cable (ρ = 7850 kg/m³, E = 200 GPa) hangs vertically under its own weight. Derive the extension and find the maximum stress and the extension.
markScheme: At distance x from the bottom, tension = ρgAx, so stress = ρgx
Maximum stress at the top = ρgL = 7.70 MPa
Element strain = ρgx/E; δ = ∫₀ᴸ ρgx/E dx = ρgL²/(2E)
Notes this is half the extension if the total weight hung at the end
questions.modelAnswer: Measure x upward from the free end. A section at x supports the cable below it, of weight ρgAx, so the stress is σ(x) = ρgx, increasing linearly to a maximum at the top of ρgL = 7850 × 9.81 × 100 = 7.70 × 10⁶ Pa = 7.70 MPa. An element dx has strain ρgx/E, so its extension is (ρgx/E)dx. Integrating from 0 to L gives δ = ρgL²/(2E) = 7850 × 9.81 × 10⁴/(4 × 10¹¹) = 1.93 × 10⁻³ m, about 1.9 mm. This is half the extension the same total weight would cause if hung from the bottom of a weightless cable, because on average each element carries only half the weight.

questions.q: For the overhanging beam (pin at A, roller at B 6 m away, 2 m overhang to C, 10 kN/m on AB, 20 kN at C; R_A = 23.33 kN), what is the maximum sagging bending moment?
questions.why: V = 23.33 − 10x = 0 at x = 2.33 m, where M = 23.33 × 2.333 − 5 × 2.333² = 27.2 kN m. 45.0 kN m is wL²/8 for a simple 6 m span, ignoring the overhang load, which reduces sagging. 40.0 kN m is the hogging moment at B, not a sagging value. 54.4 kN m is R_A × 2.333 alone, forgetting to subtract the moment of the UDL.

questions.q: For the same beam, where is the point of contraflexure on span AB?
questions.why: M = 23.33x − 5x² = 0 gives x = 23.33/5 = 4.67 m (besides x = 0 at the support). 2.33 m is where the shear is zero, i.e. the location of maximum sagging moment, not zero moment. 6.00 m is support B, where the moment is −40 kN m, not zero. 3.00 m is mid-span, which would only matter for a symmetric simply supported beam.

questions.q: A 2.5 m cantilever balcony beam carries a UDL of 6 kN/m and a 4 kN point load at its tip. Find the shear force and bending moment at the support and describe the diagrams.
markScheme: Support shear = 6 × 2.5 + 4 = 19 kN
Support moment = 6 × 2.5²/2 + 4 × 2.5 = 18.75 + 10 = 28.75 kN m hogging
SFD: linear from 4 kN at the tip to 19 kN at the support
BMD: parabolic, zero at the tip, 28.75 kN m hogging at the support (tension on top)
questions.modelAnswer: Measuring x from the tip, V(x) = 4 + 6x, so the shear rises linearly from 4 kN at the tip to 4 + 15 = 19 kN at the support. M(x) = −(4x + 3x²), hogging throughout. At the support (x = 2.5 m): M = −(10 + 18.75) = −28.75 kN m. The BMD is a parabola from zero at the tip to 28.75 kN m hogging at the wall. The top of the beam is in tension along its whole length, so in a reinforced concrete balcony the main bars go near the top surface.

questions.q: A simply supported timber joist spans 4 m and carries a UDL of 2 kN/m. If the allowable bending stress is 10 MPa, what minimum elastic section modulus is required?
questions.why: M = wL²/8 = 2 × 16/8 = 4 kN m = 4 × 10⁶ N mm; Z = M/σ = 4 × 10⁶/10 = 4 × 10⁵ mm³. 8.0 × 10⁵ mm³ treats the total load wL = 8 kN as a central point load (M = PL/4 = 8 kN m). 1.6 × 10⁶ mm³ uses wL²/2, the cantilever formula. 4.0 × 10² mm³ takes M as 4000 N m but σ in N/mm², mixing metres and millimetres (4 kN m is 4 × 10⁶ N mm).

questions.q: A beam has a T-shaped cross-section with its flange on top, and the neutral axis lies 80 mm above the base in a section 120 mm deep. Under a sagging moment, where does the largest tensile stress occur?
options: At the bottom of the web, 80 mm from the neutral axis
At the top of the flange, 40 mm from the neutral axis
At mid-depth, 60 mm above the base
questions.why: Sagging puts the bottom fibres in tension, and the bottom is the extreme fibre furthest from the neutral axis (80 mm), so it has both the tensile sign and the largest |y|. The top of the flange is in compression in sagging, and only 40 mm from the axis. The neutral axis has zero bending stress by definition. Mid-depth is not the neutral axis for an unsymmetrical section, which is the mistake of assuming the axis is always at half the depth.

questions.q: Find the second moment of area and elastic section modulus of a rectangular hollow section 100 mm wide × 200 mm deep with 10 mm walls, bent about its major axis. What bending moment causes a maximum stress of 165 MPa?
markScheme: Inner dimensions 80 × 180 mm
y_max = 100 mm, Z = 2.78 × 10⁵ mm³
M ≈ 45.8 kN m
questions.modelAnswer: The inner void is 100 − 2 × 10 = 80 mm wide and 200 − 2 × 10 = 180 mm deep. Both rectangles share the same centroid, so I = (100 × 200³ − 80 × 180³)/12 = (1.600 × 10⁹ − 0.4666 × 10⁹)/12 = 2.78 × 10⁷ mm⁴. The extreme fibre is 100 mm from the neutral axis, so Z = 2.78 × 10⁷/100 = 2.78 × 10⁵ mm³. The moment giving 165 MPa at the extreme fibres is M = σZ = 165 × 2.78 × 10⁵ = 4.58 × 10⁷ N mm = 45.8 kN m.

questions.q: A 2 m cantilever carries a UDL of 5 kN/m along its length. EI = 5000 kN m². What is the tip deflection?
questions.why: δ = wL⁴/(8EI) = 5 × 16/(8 × 5000) = 0.002 m = 2.0 mm. 5.3 mm treats the total load wL = 10 kN as a tip point load (PL³/(3EI) = 10 × 8/15 000). 0.21 mm uses the simply supported formula 5wL⁴/(384EI). 16 mm omits the factor 8 in the denominator.

questions.q: Which pair of boundary conditions is used to find the constants of integration for a simply supported beam of span L?
options: v = 0 at x = 0 and v = 0 at x = L
M = 0 and V = 0 at x = L
questions.why: Pins and rollers prevent vertical movement but allow rotation, so the deflection is zero at both supports while the slopes are free. Zero deflection and slope at x = 0 are the conditions for a fixed (cantilever) end. Zero slope at both supports would describe a beam with both ends fixed against rotation. M = 0 and V = 0 are force conditions for a free end; they are used to write M(x), not to fix the integration constants of the deflection.

questions.q: Using Macaulay's method, find the mid-span deflection of a simply supported beam of span 6 m with 10 kN point loads at x = 2 m and x = 4 m. EI = 20 000 kN m².
markScheme: Reactions 10 kN each
Integrate twice with brackets intact; v(0) = 0 gives C₂ = 0
v(6) = 0 gives C₁ = −40 kN m²
At x = 3: EI v = 45 − 1.67 − 120 = −76.7 kN m³, v = −3.83 mm (downward)
Checks against 23PL³/(648EI)
questions.modelAnswer: By symmetry each reaction is 10 kN. With x from A, sagging positive and v upward: EI v″ = M = 10x − 10⟨x − 2⟩ − 10⟨x − 4⟩. Integrating: EI v′ = 5x² − 5⟨x − 2⟩² − 5⟨x − 4⟩² + C₁, and EI v = (5/3)x³ − (5/3)⟨x − 2⟩³ − (5/3)⟨x − 4⟩³ + C₁x + C₂. At x = 0 all terms vanish, so C₂ = 0. At x = 6: (5/3)(216 − 64 − 8) + 6C₁ = 0, so 240 + 6C₁ = 0 and C₁ = −40 kN m². At mid-span x = 3 (the ⟨x − 4⟩ term is zero): EI v = 45 − 1.667 − 120 = −76.67 kN m³, so v = −76.67/20 000 = −3.83 × 10⁻³ m: 3.83 mm downward. This agrees with the standard result 23PL³/(648EI) = 3.83 mm.

questions.q: A strut has an Euler buckling load of 72 kN when pinned at both ends. What is its buckling load if it is instead fixed at the base and free at the top?
questions.why: Fixed–free gives L_e = 2L, and P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², so P_cr = 72/4 = 18 kN. 36 kN divides by 2 instead of 2², forgetting that the length is squared. 144 kN multiplies by 2 instead of dividing by 4: it applies the length factor the wrong way round (as if the effective length halved) and also forgets to square it. 288 kN is the fixed–fixed value (L_e = 0.5L), the opposite end condition.

questions.q: A rectangular timber strut is 50 mm × 100 mm in section and pinned at both ends. About which axis does it buckle, and why?
options: About the axis parallel to the 100 mm side, because that gives the smaller I
About the axis parallel to the 50 mm side, because that gives the larger I
About whichever axis the load is closest to
It cannot buckle because timber is not a metal
questions.why: The strut buckles about the axis with the minimum I. Bending about the axis parallel to the 100 mm side makes 50 mm the depth: I = 100 × 50³/12 = 1.04 × 10⁶ mm⁴, a quarter of 50 × 100³/12 = 4.17 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Choosing the larger I reverses the logic and overestimates P_cr fourfold. For an ideal axially loaded strut the load position does not pick the axis; the section stiffness does. Buckling is an elastic stability effect that applies to any slender member, whatever the material.

questions.q: A 3 m pin-ended steel tube has outside diameter 60 mm and inside diameter 50 mm (E = 200 GPa, σ_y = 275 MPa). Find its slenderness ratio, Euler buckling load and squash load, and state which governs.
markScheme: P_cr = π²EI/L² = 72.2 kN
Squash load = 275 × 864 = 238 kN
Buckling governs (λ above the limiting value of about 85; P_cr < squash load)
questions.modelAnswer: A = π(3600 − 2500)/4 = 864 mm². I = π(60⁴ − 50⁴)/64 = π × (12 960 000 − 6 250 000)/64 = π × 6.71 × 10⁶/64 = 3.29 × 10⁵ mm⁴. r = √(3.29 × 10⁵/864) = 19.5 mm, so λ = 3000/19.5 = 154. Euler load: P_cr = π² × 200 000 × 3.29 × 10⁵/3000² = 7.22 × 10⁴ N = 72.2 kN, a critical stress of 83.6 MPa. Squash load = 275 × 864 = 238 kN. The Euler load is far lower, and λ = 154 exceeds the limiting slenderness π√(200 000/275) ≈ 85, so elastic buckling governs. In practice imperfections would reduce the capacity somewhat further.

questions.q:
A steel beam ABC is pinned at A, rests on a roller at B (6 m from A) and overhangs 2 m to a free end C. It carries a UDL of 10 kN/m over AB and a 20 kN point load at C. The beam is a symmetric I-section 300 mm deep with I = 8.0 × 10⁷ mm⁴.
(a) Find the support reactions. [4]
(b) Draw the shear force and bending moment diagrams, giving all key values, the position and value of the maximum sagging moment, and the position of the point of contraflexure. [11]
(c) Find the maximum tensile and compressive bending stresses, stating where each occurs. [6]
(d) If the allowable bending stress is 165 MPa, what minimum elastic section modulus would be needed? Comment on the given section. [4]
markScheme: (a) R_B = 340/6 = 56.67 kN; R_A = 23.33 kN; checked by a second equation
(b) SF: +23.33 at A, zero at 2.33 m, −36.67 just left of B, +20 just right of B to C
(b) M = 23.33x − 5x² on AB; M_max sag = 27.2 kN m at x = 2.33 m
(b) M_B = −40 kN m (hogging), linear to zero at C
(b) Contraflexure at x = 4.67 m
(c) Largest |M| = 40 kN m at B: σ = 40 × 10⁶ × 150/8 × 10⁷ = 75 MPa, tension at the top and compression at the bottom over B
(c) Under max sagging: σ = 27.2 × 10⁶ × 150/8 × 10⁷ = 51 MPa, tension at the bottom, compression at the top
(d) Z ≥ 40 × 10⁶/165 = 2.42 × 10⁵ mm³; given Z = 5.33 × 10⁵ mm³, so the section is adequate in bending with a margin
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Moments about A: 6R_B = 60 × 3 + 20 × 8 = 340, so R_B = 56.67 kN. Vertical equilibrium: R_A = 60 + 20 − 56.67 = 23.33 kN. Check with moments about B: 6R_A = 60 × 3 − 20 × 2 = 140, R_A = 23.33 kN.

(b) Shear force: on AB, V = 23.33 − 10x, falling from +23.33 kN at A, through zero at x = 2.333 m, to −36.67 kN just left of B. At B the reaction raises it by 56.67 to +20 kN, which stays constant to C and falls to zero at the free end under the 20 kN load. Bending moment: on AB, M = 23.33x − 5x². This is zero at A, reaches its maximum where V = 0: M = 23.33 × 2.333 − 5 × 2.333² = 54.44 − 27.22 = 27.2 kN m (sagging), returns to zero at x = 23.33/5 = 4.67 m (the point of contraflexure), and reaches −40 kN m at B (check: 23.33 × 6 − 5 × 36 = −40). On BC, M = −20 × (distance from C), a straight line from −40 kN m at B to zero at C. The BMD is therefore a parabola on AB, sagging then hogging, followed by a straight line on the overhang.

(c) The greatest moment in magnitude is the 40 kN m hogging moment at B. With y_max = 150 mm: σ = 40 × 10⁶ × 150/8.0 × 10⁷ = 75 MPa, tensile in the top flange and compressive in the bottom flange over support B. In the span, the maximum sagging moment gives σ = 27.2 × 10⁶ × 150/8.0 × 10⁷ = 51 MPa, tensile in the bottom flange and compressive in the top flange at 2.33 m from A. Since the section is symmetric, the overall maxima are 75 MPa tension and 75 MPa compression, both over B.

(d) Z_required = M_max/σ_allow = 40 × 10⁶/165 = 2.42 × 10⁵ mm³. The given section has Z = I/y_max = 8.0 × 10⁷/150 = 5.33 × 10⁵ mm³, more than twice the requirement, so it is adequate in bending (stress ratio 75/165 = 0.45). A full design would also check shear, deflection (especially at the tip of the overhang) and lateral–torsional buckling of the compression flange, which near B is the bottom flange.

questions.q:
A Pratt truss spans 8 m with four 2 m panels and a height of 2 m (bottom joints A–E, top joints F, G, H above B, C, D; diagonals A–F, F–C, C–H, H–E). It is pinned at A, on a roller at E, and carries 10 kN at each of B, C and D. All members are steel tubes, 60 mm outside and 50 mm inside diameter (A = 864 mm², I = 3.29 × 10⁵ mm⁴, E = 200 GPa).
(a) Show that the truss is statically determinate. [2]
(b) Find the forces in AF, AB, BF, FG, FC, BC and CG, stating tension or compression. [9]
(c) Check the most critical compression member for Euler buckling (pinned ends) and give its factor of safety. [6]
(d) Find the stress and extension of member BC. [3]
markScheme: (a) m = 13, r = 3, j = 8: m + r = 16 = 2j; triangulated, so stable and determinate
(b) Reactions 15 kN each; F_AF = −21.2 kN (C), F_AB = +15 kN (T), F_BF = +10 kN (T)
(b) Section: F_FG = −20 kN (C), F_BC = +15 kN (T), F_FC = +7.07 kN (T); F_CG = 0 by joint G
(c) Candidates: AF (21.2 kN, L = 2.83 m) and FG (20 kN, L = 2 m)
(c) P_cr(AF) = π²EI/L² = 81.3 kN, factor of safety 3.8
(c) P_cr(FG) = 162.5 kN, factor 8.1, so AF is critical
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) There are m = 13 members (4 bottom chord, 2 top chord, 3 verticals, 4 diagonals), j = 8 joints and r = 3 reactions (pin 2, roller 1). m + r = 16 = 2j, and the truss is built from triangles, so it is stable and statically determinate.

(b) By symmetry R_A = R_E = 15 kN. Joint A: vertically, F_AF sin 45° + 15 = 0, so F_AF = −21.2 kN (compression); horizontally, F_AB = −F_AF cos 45° = 15 kN (tension). Joint B: vertically, F_BF = 10 kN (tension); horizontally, F_BC = F_AB = 15 kN (tension). Section through FG, FC and BC (left part): moments about C give 2F_FG = −(15 × 4 − 10 × 2), so F_FG = −20 kN (compression); moments about F give 2F_BC = 15 × 2, confirming F_BC = 15 kN; vertical equilibrium gives 15 − 10 − F_FC sin 45° = 0, so F_FC = 7.07 kN (tension). Joint G is unloaded with FG and GH collinear, so F_CG = 0.

(c) The compression members are AF (and HE), 21.2 kN over 2√2 = 2.83 m, and FG (and GH), 20 kN over 2 m. Pinned-end Euler loads: AF: P_cr = π² × 200 000 × 3.29 × 10⁵/2828² = 81.3 kN, factor of safety 81.3/21.2 = 3.8. FG: P_cr = π² × 200 000 × 3.29 × 10⁵/2000² = 162.5 kN, factor 8.1. AF is the critical member: although its force is similar, its greater length halves its buckling load. The compressive stress in AF is only 24.6 MPa, far below yield, confirming that buckling, not strength, governs.

(d) σ_BC = 15 000/864 = 17.4 MPa (tension). Extension δ = σL/E = 17.4 × 2000/200 000 = 0.17 mm.
